Baby & Child

Does ADHD run in families? What a parent’s diagnosis tells you

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

After receiving an ADHD diagnosis, a parent remembers losing schoolbooks and struggling to get started on assignments. Their child has just left a lunchbox at school for the third time. It is reasonable to wonder about a family link. The parent’s history is worth sharing, and the child’s own experience deserves a look of its own.

What can pass from parent to child?

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) tends to run in families. Having a parent or sibling with ADHD increases a child’s likelihood of having it. For most families there is no single ADHD gene and no simple inheritance rule that gives a reliable percentage for one child. A child can have ADHD even when no relative has a diagnosis.

Many genetic differences each contribute a small part of the variation in risk across a population. Families also share environments and experiences. A figure describing how much variation is associated with genetic differences in a group cannot tell you what fraction of one child’s difficulties came from either parent. Two siblings, including twins, may have different strengths and different needs.

What a genetic study actually measured

In a large study, researchers compared genetic data from 38,691 people with ADHD and 186,843 people in a comparison group. They identified 27 regions of the genome associated with ADHD. Finding a difference more often in one group is evidence about patterns across many people. It does not establish which child in a family will have the condition.

Occasionally attention difficulties are part of a broader genetic condition. A clinician may investigate other developmental or physical findings when they are present. For the usual question about ADHD in a family, a DNA result or a brain image cannot establish the diagnosis. The clinical assessment looks at development, symptoms and their effects in everyday life.

A family resemblance is a reason to ask questions

Misplacing a lunchbox is common. Notice what else happens, how often and with what effect. Does the child regularly miss parts of instructions even during activities they want to do? Do difficulties waiting or keeping track of belongings repeatedly get in the way of lessons or friendships? Consider what is expected for their age and what helps them manage.

Ask a teacher or caregiver for a concrete example, including a time things went well. A child who seems quiet can have difficulty sustaining attention. A child who moves a lot may be concentrating well. If problems repeatedly interfere with daily life, take the examples and family history to the child’s healthcare professional. No family history is required to ask for help.

What to tell the clinician

Explain who in the family has been diagnosed and whether the child has difficulties in more than one setting. Include when you first noticed them, changes in sleep or hearing, how learning is going and any relevant medical history. Anxiety, sleep difficulties or learning needs can resemble attention problems or occur alongside them.

Researchers also study associations with circumstances such as complications around birth or exposure to lead. A risk factor cannot establish the cause of one child’s symptoms. Raise a specific exposure with the clinician if it concerns you. Decisions about assessment and support depend on the child’s actual difficulties and strengths.

Support can start with a practical problem

Ask your child what would help them remember the lunchbox. They might choose a bright pocket in the bag or a picture by the classroom door. Try one change with the teacher and see whether it makes the end of the day easier. It can help whether or not a diagnosis follows.

If ADHD is diagnosed, ask which supports suit the child’s age and needs. Parent training in behaviour management, support at school and, when appropriate, prescribed medication are options. Your own treatment history may give you questions to ask. Your child needs an individual plan and follow-up.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Share the family history alongside observations of the child in their own right.

Use evidence from more than one setting when investigating attention difficulties.

Discuss the purpose of any proposed test and what would change the child’s care.

How BeMama can help

BeMama follows a forgotten lunchbox from a parent’s question about inheritance to a conversation with school and a practical change the child can choose.

When to seek help

Seek a professional assessment when attention or impulse-control difficulties repeatedly interfere with daily life. A genetic report or a relative’s response to a medicine cannot determine a child’s diagnosis or treatment.

Sources and further reading

  • MedlinePlus Genetics, US National Library of Medicine — Genetics and inheritance of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
  • Demontis and colleagues, Nature Genetics — Genome-wide analysis of genetic regions associated with ADHD
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — How professionals diagnose ADHD
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Treatment of ADHD

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A close relative’s ADHD increases likelihood but cannot predict a particular child’s diagnosis.
  • Genetic findings from groups do not yield an at-home diagnostic test.
  • Bring real examples from home and school and describe how they affect daily life.
  • Support a difficult daily routine while arranging an assessment when needed.

Frequently asked questions

Which children have a higher likelihood of ADHD?

A close relative with ADHD is one clue. Genetic differences and environmental or developmental factors can contribute. A risk factor alone cannot show why one child is struggling or whether they have ADHD.

If I have ADHD, will my child inherit it?

Your child’s likelihood is higher than it would be without that family history, but inheritance for most families has no simple pattern. One parent, both parents or neither parent may have been diagnosed. Tell the clinician what you know about your family.

Which signs should I mention?

Describe persistent difficulty paying attention, following through, waiting or controlling impulses when it affects daily life. Include examples in different settings. An occasional forgotten item, restlessness during a long wait or a baby’s activity level cannot make the diagnosis.

Can a child with ADHD be helped?

Yes. A healthcare professional can assess the pattern, consider other explanations and help the family choose strategies, school support or treatment. Ask what to try first and when to review progress.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
